title: SYSK’s Fall True Crime Playlist: How The Great Train Robbery Worked
summary: Chuck and Josh cover the 1963 Great Train Robbery in England, in which a gang of about fifteen men stopped the Up Special mail train near Leighton Buzzard and took roughly 2.6 million pounds in cash. They explain the Bowler Hat Gang and South Coast Raiders, the inside man Ulsterman (identified as Patrick McKenna), the rigged signal, the conductor Jack Mills being coshed, the hideout at Leathers Slade Farm, the police Flying Squad investigation, the trials and harsh thirty-year sentences, Bowl's wrongful conviction, and the later lives of the robbers, including Ronald Biggs's escapes, life in Brazil, and return to Britain. The episode ends with listener mail about horse milk (kumis) from Kazakhstan. This is part of a true crime playlist.

segments.title: Playlist intro
segments.summary: Host teaser introducing the episode as the last in a true crime playlist on the 1963 Great Train Robbery in Britain.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts chat about Chuck's cold, their trip to Vancouver, and documentaries and films about the robbery such as The Tale of Two Thieves.

segments.title: Background of the 1963 heist
segments.summary: Context: the 1855 gold train robbery as an earlier comparison, and why the 1963 robbery became a crime of the century in England and made its robbers working-class heroes.

segments.title: Ronald Biggs as folk hero
segments.summary: Biggs spent about thirty years on the run and became an anti-establishment folk figure; street interviews showed public sympathy for the robbers.

segments.title: Forming the gang and choosing the train
segments.summary: Fields pitched the idea; safecracker Gordon Goody joined. The Bowler Hat Gang, led by Bruce Reynolds, teamed with the South Coast Raiders led by Buster Edwards after a failed earlier train attempt. They targeted the Up Special, a mail sorting train running from Glasgow to London since the 1830s.

segments.title: Lax security on mail train
segments.summary: The Up Special carried mail and cash with no armed guards or alarms, staffed mostly by postmen, which surprised the hosts.

segments.title: Ulsterman inside man
segments.summary: The inside man code-named Ulsterman was named by Gordon Goody as Patrick McKenna, revealed in the documentary A Tale of Two Thieves; the family says he later gave his share to the Catholic Church.

segments.title: Bank holiday timing and cash amount
segments.summary: The inside man suggested the August 1963 bank holiday timing for a bigger take. The train carried about 300,000 pounds nightly, but on August 8, 1963 it carried about 2.6 million pounds.

segments.title: Gang members and accomplices
segments.summary: Beyond the core gang, accomplices Mister One, Two and Three were involved; John Wheeler got away and provided the safe house.

segments.title: Rigging the signal and failed train driver
segments.summary: Roger Cordrey devised rigging the red signal with a glove over the green light. The hired elderly driver could not operate the handbrake, so the conductor Jack Mills was attacked with a cosh and forced to drive another mile and a half to the drop point at Bridego bridge.

segments.title: Conductor injuries and the attacker's identity
segments.summary: Jack Mills never fully recovered, had headaches, and died years later. James Hussey reportedly confessed on his deathbed to the assault, but Mills's son disputes it.

segments.title: Gordon Goody's book and Buster film
segments.summary: Goody's book named Buster Edwards or James Hussey as the attacker. The hosts mention the film Buster about Edwards.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Break between segments.

segments.title: The heist and getaway to the farmhouse
segments.summary: The gang offloaded about 120 sacks of cash in roughly fifteen minutes onto a lorry and Land Rovers, then fled to a prearranged hideout at Leathers Slade Farm bought by Fields. Police put out a thirty-mile search radius.

segments.title: Hideout mistakes
segments.summary: A neighbor reported suspicious activity at the farm. The gang stayed about eight days, played Monopoly with real money, left prints and ketchup bottles behind, and left early because the planned torching never happened.

segments.title: Flying Squad investigation and informant
segments.summary: Scotland Yard's Flying Squad, led by Tommy Butler, arrested gang members quickly. Informant Mickey Kejo was said to have named names, which the robbers deny.

segments.title: Silence during the arrests
segments.summary: Most arrested robbers stayed tight-lipped; treasurer Charlie Wilson, called the silent man, said nothing at trial.

segments.title: Arrests and trial
segments.summary: Twelve of fifteen were rounded up by August. Biggs was tried separately because of his criminal record. Ten stood trial, and one was acquitted after lawyers showed his fingerprints on the Monopoly game could have been left earlier.

segments.title: Disputed evidence and false confessions
segments.summary: Evidence included yellow paint on a shoe and a hastily painted yellow lorry. Goody later admitted painting the truck. Claims of planted evidence and false confessions were made.

segments.title: Bowl William Bowl's wrongful conviction
segments.summary: Bowl William Bowl received fourteen years despite having little involvement; he had been paid a debt and helped a friend lay low. Roger Cordrey was caught first after a garage rental suspicion. Bowl died in prison, and his family is seeking a posthumous pardon.

segments.title: Sentences and judge
segments.summary: Robbers received around thirty-year sentences, double the previous harshest robbery penalties. Judge Edmund Davies gave harsh sentences here while reducing a sentence in a separate killing case.

segments.title: Prison escapes and Biggs in Brazil
segments.summary: Several robbers escaped prison, including Charlie Wilson and Biggs from Wandsworth Prison. Biggs had plastic surgery, went to Australia then Brazil, and avoided extradition because his child was Brazilian.

segments.title: Jack Slipper pursuit and remaining robbers
segments.summary: Detective Jack Slipper pursued Biggs; Biggs lived openly in Brazil. Most other robbers were caught by 1969, except the three unidentified accomplices. Mastermind Bruce Reynolds evaded police for years, and Buster Edwards turned himself in after three years.

segments.title: Name change and Colin Firth tangent
segments.summary: Bruce Reynolds changed his family surname to Firth while on the run. The hosts joke about a link to actor Colin Firth, which is coincidental.

segments.title: Money recovery and currency change
segments.summary: About 400,000 pounds of the 2.6 million was recovered. The government considered reissuing banknotes, and England later changed currency, making unrecovered notes worthless. Money was reportedly laundered through bookies.

segments.title: Fates of the robbers and Biggs's final years
segments.summary: Several robbers died violently or under unhappy circumstances, including one killed by a hitman in Spain. Biggs was kidnapped from Brazil in 1981 by ex-military men, freed in Barbados, returned to Brazil, and eventually returned to Britain in 2001 where he died in 2013. Goody wrote a book.

segments.title: Pointer to search and transition
segments.summary: Hosts suggest further reading via the search bar and move to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail: horse milk
segments.summary: Listeners respond to the earlier horse milk episode, describing kumis from Kazakhstan as sour, mildly alcoholic fermented horse milk, and a listener who tried it describing it served in a bowl.

segments.summary: Hosts give ways to contact the show and sign off.
